nodes.name: 'More' means a greater number, not bigger things
nodes.statement: When two collections are compared, 'more' refers to the number of objects in each, not to the size of the objects or the space they cover.
nodes.assess: Show 3 large balls spread across the table and 9 small marbles in a tight cluster. 'Which group has more?' Credit the marbles.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement says 'more' refers to the number in each group, and the learner finds those numbers by counting each group.
Matching objects one to one shows which group has leftover objects, so 'more' is judged by number and not by size or spread.
The learner must already judge which of two very unequal sets has more before the meaning of 'more' can be tied to number rather than size.

nodes.name: A shape's boundary closes with no gaps
nodes.statement: A flat shape such as a triangle or a square is bounded by a line that goes all the way around and meets itself; a figure whose boundary has a gap is not that shape.
nodes.assess: Show 6 drawings of fences: three closed triangles and squares, and the same three figures each with a small gap in one side or corner. 'Which fences have no gap, so the sheep inside cannot get out?' Credit all and only the three closed figures.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement contrasts a complete triangle or square with a gapped figure, so the learner must already see the intended shape.

nodes.name: Pick out the shape that is named
nodes.statement: When the name circle, square, or triangle is said, pick out a typical example of that shape from a set of shapes.
nodes.assess: Lay out a typical circle, square, triangle, and rectangle, each resting on a side. 'Show me the triangle.' Repeat for the circle and the square. Credit the correct shape each time.

proposed_edges.rationale: Picking the named shape from a set means the child already sees which shapes are the same shape and which are different.

nodes.name: Form the digits 0 to 9
nodes.statement: Write each of the digits 0 through 9 so that it is recognizable and not reversed.
nodes.assess: Show a card with the digits 0 to 9. 'Copy each number onto your paper.' Credit all ten digits legible and none reversed.

nodes.name: Know the number words zero to nine as words
nodes.statement: The words zero through nine are number words, each one a separate word the learner can say and tell apart from other words, whether or not the learner can recite them in order.
nodes.assess: Say these words one at a time: 'seven, blue, cat, three, zero, run, nine'. 'Clap when you hear a number word.' Credit claps for seven, three, zero, and nine only.

nodes.name: Spreading out or pushing together does not change how many
nodes.statement: Moving the objects of a collection closer together or farther apart, without adding or removing any, does not change how many objects there are.
nodes.assess: Lay out two rows of 6 counters, matched one to one, and the child agrees the rows have the same number. While the child watches, spread one row out so it is longer. 'Does one row have more now, or do they have the same number?' Credit 'the same', given without counting.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test starts from two rows matched one to one, and the child must see that matching shows the same number.
The test question asks whether one row has more now, so the child must take 'more' to mean number, not length.
Knowing a count stays the same however the objects are arranged supports judging that spreading out leaves how many unchanged.

nodes.name: Count a group of objects as one unit
nodes.statement: A group of objects, such as a pair of socks or a bundle of ten sticks, can be counted as one unit, so that the count tells how many groups there are rather than how many objects.
nodes.assess: Show 4 pairs of socks, each pair clipped together. 'How many socks are there? How many pairs of socks are there?' Credit 8 socks and 4 pairs.

proposed_edges.rationale: Counting the pairs gives how many groups and counting the socks gives how many objects, so the child must already count a collection.

nodes.name: Partition a strip or segment into equal lengths
nodes.statement: Partition a strip or segment into b parts of equal length that together fill it, with no gaps or overlaps.
nodes.assess: Give the child a paper strip. 'Fold or mark this strip into 4 parts that are all the same length.' Credit four equal parts that fill the whole strip, checked by laying one part along the others.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test checks the equal parts by laying one part along the others, which is a direct comparison of lengths.
The statement asks for parts of equal length, so length must already be an attribute the child can attend to.
The parts must together fill the whole strip with no gaps or overlaps, the same idea as spanning a length.
The requirement that parts together fill the strip with no gaps or overlaps is the whole being all of its equal shares.

nodes.name: Compare a fraction with 1 by its numerator and denominator
nodes.statement: A fraction a/b is greater than 1 when a is greater than b, equal to 1 when a equals b, and less than 1 when a is less than b.
nodes.assess: Without computing, sort these fractions into less than 1, equal to 1, and greater than 1: 3/5, 7/4, 6/6, 9/10, 5/2. Credit all five placed correctly.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement itself compares the whole numbers a and b as greater than, equal to, or less than.
The rule follows by comparing a/b with b/b, two fractions with the same denominator, by their numerators a and b.
Reading a/b as a copies of 1/b, and knowing that b copies of 1/b make 1, gives the comparison with 1.
Comparing a/b with 1 uses 1 written as b/b, so the equal-to-1 case rests on whole numbers written as fractions.

nodes.name: A complex fraction as a division of fractions
nodes.statement: A fraction whose numerator and denominator are themselves fractions, (a/b)/(c/d), means a/b divided by c/d.
nodes.assess: Rewrite (1/2)/(3/4) as a division expression using the division sign.

proposed_edges.rationale: The numerator and denominator are themselves fractions, which only makes sense if a fraction is a number.
The statement extends the meaning of a fraction bar as division, a divided by b equals a/b, to a bar between two fractions.

nodes.name: Recall division facts within 100
nodes.statement: Recall the quotient of a divided by b whenever a = b x c with b and c whole numbers from 1 to 10.
nodes.assess: 'Tell me the answers: 56 divided by 8, 42 divided by 6, 81 divided by 9.' Credit all three correct, each given without counting or computing aloud.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement defines the quotient through a = b x c, which is a quotient seen as an unknown factor.
Recalling a divided by b rests on knowing the fluent multiplication fact b x c = a for single-digit factors.

nodes.name: A decrease as a negative number
nodes.statement: A decrease in a quantity is written as a negative number whose size is the amount of the decrease, and an increase as a positive number.
nodes.assess: The water in a tank goes down by 15 liters. Write the change in the amount of water as a signed number. Credit -15.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement writes a decrease with a negative number, so the learner must already know a negative number as the opposite of a positive amount.
